Threespot leporinus (Leporinus friderici) exhibits a set of life-history traits typical of many Neotropical characiforms. Upon hatching, the free-embryo is minute; field observations suggest that the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0005 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0005 grams], a value derived from an average egg diameter of one millimeter. This tiny mass belies a rapid juvenile growth phase that is strongly influenced by water temperature. The species eventually attains a maximum recorded body mass of 974 grams [Wwi = 974 grams], which represents the largest individuals observed in pristine river systems. Corresponding to this maximum weight, the ultimate total length of the threespot leporinus is approximately 40 centimeters [Li = approximately 40 centimeters], placing it among the larger-bodied members of its genus in South American floodplain habitats. These upper limits on size are achieved only by older, dominant individuals that have access to productive foraging grounds.

Reproductive activity in Leporinus friderici commences when individuals reach a distinct size threshold. Measurements from gonad inspection campaigns indicate that the total length at puberty is 18.1 centimeters [Lp = 18.1 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at sexual maturation of roughly 85.3 grams [Wwp = roughly 85.3 grams]. This weight is calculated using a length-weight relationship derived from long-term sampling of the population. Attaining this stage marks the transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes periodic investment in gamete production. Individuals below this size are consistently immature, with no evidence of vitellogenesis or advanced spermatogenesis, whereas specimens exceeding this length frequently display signs of active gonadal recrudescence. The concordance between these two metrics reinforces their utility for defining the onset of reproductive capability in field-based demographic models.

The maximum reproductive output of this species has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, female threespot leporinus are capable of producing approximately 117189 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 117189 eggs per year], a value representing the upper bound of annual fecundity. This high rate of oviposition is sustained during the peak of the spawning season and reflects the species' strategy of producing numerous small, pelagic eggs that undergo external fertilisation during flood pulses. The rate is among the highest recorded for characiforms of comparable body size and is likely an adaptation to high larval mortality in dynamic riverine environments. Egg production declines markedly outside of the optimal thermal window, and field data suggest that wild populations rarely sustain this maximum rate for extended periods. The interplay between temperature and food availability modulates this reproductive ceiling in natural habitats.

Longevity estimates for Leporinus friderici in its natural environment indicate a lifespan of approximately 5475 days [am = approximately 5475 days], again under the thermal regime characteristic of central Amazonian streams at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C]. This corresponds to roughly fifteen years, a duration that is considerable for a freshwater teleost of its size and aligns with a life-history strategy that prioritizes iteroparity over a single, catastrophic reproductive event. The oldest individuals encountered in mark-recapture studies often exhibit slower growth rates during their later years, suggesting that somatic investment declines as reproductive senescence begins. This extended lifespan allows multiple spawning opportunities across several breeding seasons, buffering the population against years of poor recruitment caused by unpredictable hydrological conditions. The link between stable thermal conditions and prolonged survival is a common pattern observed among Neotropical characiforms inhabiting low-variability environments.

Comparative analysis of Leporinus friderici with sympatric congeners reveals notable differences in both growth trajectories and reproductive timing. The sustained attainment of 974 grams [Wwi = 974 grams] in undisturbed habitats contrasts with lower maxima observed in fragmented systems, indicating the influence of habitat quality on ultimate body size. The onset of sexual maturation at 85.3 grams [Wwp = 85.3 grams] occurs earlier in proportional terms than in several related species. In laboratory experiments conducted at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the high annual egg production of approximately 117189 eggs [Ri = annual egg production of approximately 117189 eggs] remains a consistent feature, a fecundity that contrasts with the more pulse-limited reproduction observed in species inhabiting cooler headwater streams. Interestingly, the small wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0005 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0005 grams] is consistent across the genus, implying that selective pressures on egg size are conserved within the clade. The ultimate total length of approximately 40 centimeters [Li = approximately 40 centimeters] is also comparable to that reported for Leporinus elongatus, suggesting similar biomechanical constraints on body elongation.
